performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
intro: In Frühlingstraum, the eleventh song of Schubert’s Winterreise, D. 911, a dream of May flowers and a lover’s embrace ends at a cockcrow. Hans Duhan and Ferdinand Foll perform it.

sections.label: Intro · Piano introduction in 6/8
sections.mNote: Soft broken chords accompany the melody in the piano

sections.label: A · May flowers and birdsong
sections.mNote: The voice enters over the piano’s rhythm.

sections.label: B · Schnell, cockcrow, short piano chords
sections.mNote: Schnell: short piano chords end the dream section.

sections.label: C · Langsam, repeated chords, 2/4
sections.mNote: Langsam: repeated chords in a slower 2/4.

sections.label: A′ · Dream music returns, with a lover
sections.mNote: The piano returns to the opening 6/8 (Wie oben).

sections.label: B′ · Schnell; cockcrow wakes the heart
sections.mNote: Schnell returns, with clipped chords in the piano.

sections.label: C′ · Final slow verse, minor
sections.mNote: The final slow verse ends in the minor.

cues.title: First stanza, A major
cues.text: The piano begins pp in A major and 6/8, marked Etwas bewegt. The singer dreams of bright flowers, green meadows and noisy birds. Schubert sets this imaginary May morning to an easy, dance-like step.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder transcription, bars 1–13: Etwas bewegt, 6/8, A major, pp. Wilhelm Müller, Frühlingstraum, first stanza; German text at https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2. Score: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second stanza, Schnell
cues.text: “Da war es kalt und finster”: it was cold and dark. A cock’s crow has woken the wanderer, and ravens shriek on the roof. Schubert marks the passage Schnell (fast) and replaces the swaying piano figure with short chords separated by rests.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Frühlingstraum, second stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation of the German at https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2. OpenScore Lieder, bars 14–26, Schnell and clipped piano chords: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third stanza, Langsam
cues.text: At bar 27 the tempo changes to Langsam in 2/4. The piano repeats chords over a sustained A while the singer looks at the leaves painted by frost on his window, the flowers of his dream. He imagines people laughing at a man who sees flowers in winter.
cues.evidence: Müller, Frühlingstraum, third stanza, German text at https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2. OpenScore Lieder, bars 27–43: Langsam, 2/4, repeated chords with a sustained A: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening music
cues.text: At bar 44, marked Wie oben, the piano brings back the opening 6/8; the voice enters at bar 48. In this stanza the dream contains a young woman, kisses and love returned.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bar 44, Wie oben and 6/8; piano introduction through bar 47 and voice from bar 48. Müller, fourth stanza: https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2. Score: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Frühlingstraum, longest side, 1928
cues.text: At 4:11, Frühlingstraum is the longest song in Duhan and Foll’s 1928 set, which HMV issued as twelve records with each song on one side. A 12-inch shellac side held a little over four minutes.
cues.evidence: Christian Utz, “Exzentrisch geformte Klang-Landschaften”, ZGMTH 18 (2021), section 2 and note 25: the cycle published as a set of twelve records, every song on a single side; a 12-inch shellac side lasts a little over four minutes, and the longest song in Duhan and Foll’s recording is No. 11, Frühlingstraum, at 4:11. https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx

cues.title: Second awakening, bar 58
cues.text: At bar 58, marked Schnell, the cockcrow returns with the same fast, clipped accompaniment. At the first awakening his eye opens; now his heart wakes. He sits alone and thinks about the dream.
cues.evidence: Müller, Frühlingstraum, second and fifth stanzas contrast Auge and Herze: https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2. OpenScore Lieder, Schnell at bar 58: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final stanza
cues.text: “Noch schlägt das Herz so warm” — the heart still beats so warmly. The singer closes his eyes and asks when the leaves on the window will turn green and when he will hold his beloved again. Schubert repeats the last question and ends in the minor.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Frühlingstraum, final stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation of the German at https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2. OpenScore Lieder, Langsam from bar 71, repeated question in bars 83–86, A-minor final chord at bar 88: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Piano introduction to first vocal entry
transitions.how: The piano plays soft broken chords in 6/8. The voice enters on the last quaver of bar 4 in the same pulse. Schubert’s accompaniment stays in A major as the singer begins the dream of flowers.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 1–5, vocal pickup at the end of bar 4. The edition gives the original A-major key. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603

transitions.title: The change to Schnell
transitions.to: B · Schnell, cockcrow, short piano chords
transitions.how: The last note of the dream section is followed directly by the marking Schnell. The piano changes from flowing broken chords to short, pointed strokes with rests between them. The voice tells of the cockcrow, the cold room and ravens on the roof.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 14–26; Müller, second stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603; https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2

transitions.title: Slow chords at the window
transitions.from: B · Schnell, cockcrow, short piano chords
transitions.how: At bar 27 the marking changes from Schnell to Langsam and the metre from 6/8 to 2/4. Through bars 27–30 the piano plays repeated chords, pp, around a held note while the singer looks at the window. In Schubert’s original key the A is held in both hands and the bass begins on A.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 27–30: Langsam, 2/4, pp and repeated A in the piano. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603

transitions.title: Return to the opening tempo
transitions.to: A′ · Dream music returns, with a lover
transitions.how: At bar 44 the marking Wie oben restores the opening tempo and 6/8. The piano plays four bars of the A-major music from the opening. The voice re-enters at bar 48 with Müller’s fourth stanza, a dream of kisses and returned love.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bar 44, Wie oben and 6/8; voice re-enters at bar 48. Müller, fourth stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603; https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2

transitions.title: The clipped chords return
transitions.from: A′ · Dream music returns, with a lover
transitions.to: B′ · Schnell; cockcrow wakes the heart
transitions.how: Schnell returns at bar 58. The piano resumes its short chords and rests, as it did at the end of the first dream, and they break off the second dream. In the fifth stanza Müller gave the awakening to the heart.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 58–70; Müller, fifth stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603; https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2

transitions.title: The slow chords return
transitions.from: B′ · Schnell; cockcrow wakes the heart
transitions.how: Langsam and 2/4 return with the piano’s quiet repeated chords (bars 71–88). The singer closes his eyes. The question about holding his beloved is repeated, and the final chord turns Schubert’s opening A major to A minor.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 71–88: Langsam, repeated final question, A-minor close. Müller, final stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5023603; https://oxfordsong.org/song/fr%C3%BChlingstraum-2

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 11, Frühlingstraum, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: Pickup and bars 1–88. The piano opens alone; the voice enters at the end of bar 4. The second piano introduction occupies bars 44–47, and the last two bars belong to the piano.

timeline.note: The piano opens the song in 6/8 with soft broken chords.
The voice enters over the piano, singing of a dream of May flowers and birdsong.
Wie oben restores the opening music for four bars of piano alone.
The singer returns with a dream of a lover and kisses.
The voice stops; the piano closes the song in the minor.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: Utz measures this song at 4:11, the longest side of the set; no source consulted states the performing text or the key of the transfer. The transposition from the first edition and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 386, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CK 2956, take 1 (run-out “Ck 2956” with I); side No. 11 (label number 0942032); reverse side: Einsamkeit (matrix BK 2957-2). Disc 6 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (259.24 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (259.12 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
